A groundbreaking, open-source tool is introduced to revolutionize the design of neuromorphic hardware and software. The tool enables users to develop, test, and evaluate complex systems by simulating various components, including memristive devices and models, neural networks, and learning algorithms. A novel approach to simulating memristive devices is presented, combining device-level and model-level simulations to provide accurate results. Device-level simulations utilize a comprehensive model to replicate the memristive device's complex behavior, while model-level simulations approximate the device's response using a simplified model. The tool's architecture is designed to facilitate efficient emulation of large-scale systems, leveraging memristive devices and models. The tool's capabilities are demonstrated through the emulation of a biologically-inspired neuromorphic system, with memristive devices serving as adaptive synapses. The results show that the emulated system can effectively learn and exhibit biological properties, including synaptic plasticity and spike timing dependence. The tool's flexibility is further illustrated through the emulation of a reservoir computing system, highlighting the potential of memristive devices in machine learning applications. This research paves the way for the design and development of robust neuromorphic systems, with the tool's open-source release facilitating further research and development. The diffuse cosmic infrared background's (CIB) faint signal can be detected in galaxy clusters through image analysis.  We conducted a study using CIBER images to measure the intra-halo light in galaxies by stacking multiple galaxies.  We analyzed 20 galaxy clusters with a range of redshifts (0.1 to 0.3) and masses ($10^{23.8}$ to $10^{25.1}$ M$_\odot$).  We compared our findings to predictions from galaxy formation simulations and determined the fraction of intra-halo light.  We discovered that the fraction of intra-halo light varies with galaxy luminosity, with brighter galaxies having more light within the halo than fainter ones.  We also found that the fraction of intra-halo light is higher in more massive clusters and galaxies with specific stellar masses, with some clusters having up to 80% of their total light from intra-halo light.  These results support previous studies and provide new insights into the relationship between galaxy cluster properties and the presence of intra-halo light.  They also suggest that intra-halo light is an important component of the CIB, contributing a significant fraction of its total signal. The integration of multimedia elements in lecture presentations has become a widespread trend in educational settings. However, the process of creating these presentations poses a challenge due to the need for simultaneous management of visual and auditory content. To address this issue, we have developed a dataset comprising 1500 slides from 300 unique presentations to explore the complex nature of multimodal presentations. By analyzing the effects of different presentation formats, such as text, images, videos, and audio, we have found that these components significantly impact the overall meaning and content of slides. Furthermore, we have discovered that the arrangement of presentation elements can greatly influence their interpretation, underscoring the intricate relationship between modality, presentation format, and the resulting educational outcome. To facilitate future research, we have made our dataset available for public use. Our research aims to provide a foundation for the development of advanced tools that can help educators effectively harness the power of multimedia in educational settings. Specifically, we envision the use of such tools in automating the creation of presentation content, identifying areas of potential student difficulty, and generating customized educational materials tailored to individual students' needs. To achieve these goals, we propose the use of multimodal analysis techniques that can extract relevant information from presentations and identify key relationships between different presentation components. By leveraging these tools, educators can unlock new possibilities for enhancing student engagement and improving learning outcomes. Our dataset provides a valuable resource for the development of these cutting-edge technologies. For more information, please visit our project's website at https://www.multimodaleffects.org. There, you can find our dataset, as well as a range of tools and resources for the development of multimodal analysis techniques. We invite researchers to join us in exploring the exciting possibilities that the integration of multimodal analysis can bring to the field of education. Our goal is to establish a foundation for the development of advanced multimodal analysis technologies that can revolutionize the way we create educational presentations. By working together, we can unlock the full potential of multimedia in education and create a brighter future for learning. Join us in this exciting journey of discovery and innovation!

Quantum mechanics introduces the possibility of performing interaction-free measurements, which allows for the detection of an object's presence without actually interacting with it. This is achieved through a process where an object is prevented from changing its state due to a series of weak measurements, effectively 'freezing' its state. This is shown by measuring the atom's initial position, which remains accurate regardless of the preceding pulses, thereby proving that the object's state was never truly changed. This experiment showcases an innovative application of quantum mechanics in the field of cold atom research. Furthermore, it highlights the capability of the interaction-free measurement as a means of precise control over quantum systems. This is the first time this principle has been applied to systems with multiple weak measurements, and offers a new approach to control and manipulate quantum systems. This study employs natural language processing methods to analyze honeypot command data, enabling the grouping of associated IP addresses, and subsequently the identification of botnets. By examining command sequences, the research aims to determine whether honeypot servers have executed similar commands, and if so, whether these IP addresses comprise a botnet. An algorithm developed for this purpose was tested on a honeypot server dataset, yielding an initial botnet detection success rate of around 60%. Although the research encountered some difficulties due to syntax errors in command inputs and varying server configurations, it demonstrates the potential of natural language-based methods in identifying botnets. As a result, the proposed approach has significant implications for botnet detection and the development of more sophisticated algorithms for identifying malicious IP addresses. A 3D U-Net model for brain tumor segmentation is introduced in this study, combining contextual information to enhance segmentation accuracy. The proposed model incorporates a novel fusion module that integrates multi-axis information from different MRI modalities. The fusion module's output is combined with low-frequency components of input images to form a contextual view. The contextual view is then passed through a 3D U-Net for segmentation. Performance evaluations using BraTS2018 data demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, outperforming baseline models with superior performance metrics. Implementation details are available on GitHub at https://github.com/ShashankKesar/3D-UNet-Context-Aware-Brain-Tumor-SEG. 

Keywords: Brain tumor segmentation, 3D U-Net, Context-aware fusion, Brain tumors, MRI analysis. 
Abstract. Brain tumors pose a significant threat to public health, necessitating accurate diagnosis for effective treatment. Advanced MRI imaging enables precise diagnosis, whereas manual segmentation is a labor-intensive process. To address this challenge, this research proposes a novel 3D U-Net model that leverages contextual information for accurate brain tumor segmentation. The model's performance significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving high Dice scores for non-enhancing, enhancing tumor, and total tumor segments. The model's performance metrics include Dice scores of 0.846, 0.855, and 0.859, along with average Hausdorff distances of 7.51, 6.75, and 6.82 for the respective segments. This article provides construction methods for Hadamard matrices of order $2p$ and derives such matrices from the projective planes of order $p$ known as the Pless symmetries. Notably, it offers a direct approach for creating Hadamard matrices of the size $14 \times 14$, which was previously found challenging. Furthermore, it outlines a systematic procedure for generating all possible Hadamard matrices of the size $12 \times 12$ that can be formed from the projective planes of the same order. By employing these methods, it has been discovered that there are only $24$ distinct Hadamard matrices of the size $12 \times 12$, which are unique to their underlying characteristics. Utilizing these methods, it has also been established that there exist  $24$ distinct Hadamard matrices of the size $12 \times 12$, which is consistent with the findings in reference $[1]$. Lastly, it has been demonstrated that the projective planes of order $p \equiv 3 \mod 4$ are unique up to isomorphism for all prime values of $p$ less than $16$. This research draws heavily from the work in references $[2]$, $[3]$, and $[4]$.

This white paper submits on behalf of the QCD interest group for the EIC to emphasize the EIC's potential in conducting innovative precision studies of QCD, particularly in its low-energy state. Building upon the success of RHIC, the EIC, as a high-energy electron-ion collider, will offer a novel platform for exploring the QCD landscape, where perturbative principles and phenomenological insights converge. The EIC's unique combination of beam energies, luminosity, and detector capabilities will enable groundbreaking measurements of gluon distributions, probing QCD at its most fundamental level. The white paper outlines the scientific objectives, experimental approaches, and required detector features for key QCD precision studies at the EIC, as well as considerations for future development and cost estimation. The findings are intended to serve as a foundation for the laboratory's 2023 Long Range Plan update.

The analysis of gravitational waves from continuous sources necessitates the use of specific tools, which are now widely available as standalone programs. To cater to researchers who work with continuous gravitational-wave data analysis in Octave, we have developed OctApps - a collection of software tools that can run within the Octave environment. By integrating these programs into their own research pipelines, scientists can design and test detection algorithms, simulate data, and analyze real-time signals using a consistent framework. We present OctApps as a means to bridge the gap between research institutions that primarily utilize Python and those that primarily utilize Fortran/C++ and their respective connections to continuous gravitational-wave data analysis. OctApps is available for public download, along with accompanying tutorials and example scripts. We demonstrate the functionality of OctApps by showcasing its utility in simulating data, performing Bayesian inference, and analyzing real-time signals from the GW190814 event. Furthermore, we discuss the potential of OctApps to serve as a stepping stone for researchers to transition from a Python-based environment to a Fortran/C++-based environment. GANs have become a preferred solution for generating synthetic data, but their training can be unpredictable due to multiple issues, with one critical problem being mode collapse, which occurs when the trained model fails to capture the data's diverse characteristics.  To address this, we developed a new method to identify and prevent mode collapse in GANs by analyzing how the model's parameters change during training and how these changes affect the model's performance.  Specifically, we found that a specific measure called Hessian eigenvalues can help detect mode collapse by identifying areas in the data space where the model's behavior stabilizes, and we demonstrated that our approach can improve mode collapse detection through experiments on various GAN architectures.  Our findings suggest that GANs can be effectively improved using this method, leading to better results in mode collapse prevention.  Furthermore, we found that this approach can be easily integrated into existing GAN training methods, and the results support the idea that mode collapse is a complex issue that requires a comprehensive understanding of how the model's parameters evolve during training.  Our method is now available as an open-source Python library.  To our knowledge, this is the first method to address mode collapse in this way, and the code can be found at https://github.com/PrudhviVarma-V/Mode-Prevention-GANs.  Future work will involve applying this approach to other areas in machine learning, such as neural network training. The effectiveness of liquid metal jet additive manufacturing largely depends on the precise control of the liquid metal's path during the printing process. To achieve this control, sophisticated numerical models are essential, but they come with significant computational costs. To overcome this challenge, a novel approach is presented that uses reduced-order modeling through deep neural networks to accelerate part-scale simulations. This approach is applied to the specific case of LMJAM and involves training the neural network using a detailed, finite-element based solver. The resulting neural network is able to accurately predict the part-scale flow field with a significant reduction in computational time, by as much as three orders of magnitude. Furthermore, the neural network can be used to efficiently simulate multiple scenarios and analyze their impact on the printing process. The capabilities of this approach are showcased through its application to the simulation of LMJAM trajectories and the identification of optimal parameters for successful printing. The framework presented in this research can be easily adapted to address various challenges in additive manufacturing processes. The developed framework is envisioned to enable the accelerated design and optimization of multiple AM processes. The underlying code for the proposed method is available for public access. Transformers are typically hindered by their high computational requirements, particularly when working with large input datasets. A recently developed technique known as "sparsely activated" transformers has significantly reduced the computational load, allowing it to process long sequences more efficiently than initial models. Nevertheless, sparsely activated transformers face a limitation in effectively utilizing regularization methods like dropout, as the underlying mechanism relies on fully connected and easily trainable layers. To address this issue, researchers have introduced "gating dropout", a novel regularization technique specifically designed for use with sparsely activated transformers. Gating dropout enables regularization by modifying the dropout probability of each token's input rather than its activation function, thus enabling a more efficient application of dropout. Moreover, this technique has been successfully integrated into the sparsely activated Transformer-XL model, resulting in improved performance on language modeling and long-form text summarization tasks. Specifically, this enhanced model, referred to as the sparsely activated Transformer-XL, has achieved notable improvements in accuracy, with notable gains on tasks such as long-form text summarization, where it outperformed the sparsely activated Transformer-XL model, and also demonstrated comparable performance to the densely activated Transformer-XL model, all while maintaining a reduced computational complexity. The code implementing this technique has been made publicly accessible. Furthermore, this work has been recognized with an acceptance into the ACL 2021 conference. We offer an alternative proof of Wiesand's main outcome regarding the geometric Satake functor and block decomposition through the Satake algebra, leveraging the geometric Satake equivalence. This approach enables a unified explanation of how the block decomposition of the Hecke algebra influences the geometric Satake functor's composition. Lastly, we discuss the implications of Lu's theorem on the block decomposition of the geometric Satake algebra. This outcome is a result of collaborative work with Z. Duan, Y. Liu, and Y. Su. To ensure power system security, operators must analyze various operating conditions. However, these conditions are often represented by numerous scenarios, making it difficult to develop accurate stability assessments. To mitigate this issue, researchers have been exploring dimensionality reduction techniques to condense these conditions into manageable subsets. In this study, we developed an autoencoder-based approach that utilizes power flow outcomes and load trajectory patterns to condense power system scenarios. We then compared this method to a traditional principal component analysis and demonstrated its effectiveness in identifying a limited set of representative scenarios able to capture stability performance over an extensive range of loads while maintaining computational efficiency. Our study further showed that these representative conditions can be selected based on their relevance to system operators' primary concerns and can be used to guide the prioritization of transmission upgrades. The effectiveness of our approach was validated through a case study based on the IEEE 118-bus system. Moreover, we successfully applied this approach to a real-world power system in Vietnam and found that it could be used to develop a more accurate security assessment without requiring complex optimization calculations. In robotics and autonomous vehicles, accurate place recognition from 3D LiDAR data is crucial for long-term navigation systems. Soft tissue modeling is a significant issue in multiple fields, including cardiovascular medicine. To address this problem, we developed a novel approach that utilizes biaxial testing data and a Bayesian constitutive model selection framework. This method was tested using real-world data from normal porcine aortic valves. Our results show that the proposed method can effectively select between different constitutive models, including fluid-like and viscoelastic models. It also highlights the importance of accounting for model uncertainty in soft tissue modeling. With further advancements, this method could be applied to a broader range of soft tissues and materials. To access the associated code, please visit https://github.com/ChrisRipman/bayesian-constitutive-model-selection. A detailed description of the methodology and results can be found in the associated report.

Link prediction in knowledge graphs has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its numerous applications. The conventional approach to this task involves learning to recognize correlations between entities and their attributes, but this method falls short in capturing complex relationships between entities. In an attempt to address this limitation, researchers have recently focused on utilizing knowledge graphs to identify connections between entities. Nonetheless, these methods overlook the importance of detailed descriptions provided in the knowledge graph, which are crucial in understanding various types of relationships. In an effort to bridge this gap, this paper proposes a novel framework that integrates both entity descriptions and their interactions to facilitate link prediction. The proposed framework, which is based on the concept of semantic correlation, utilizes a deep learning model to learn representations of entities, descriptions, and their interactions. The link prediction process involves the computation of semantic correlation scores between entities, which are then used to determine the likelihood of connection between them. Experiments conducted on three benchmark datasets have demonstrated the efficacy of the proposed method, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, this paper provides a comprehensive ablation study to validate the importance of each component of the framework. The link prediction code developed as part of this work will be made available on the GitHub repository linked to the author's user page. We begin with a simplified model of the IPT, characterized by a weak scale symmetry, and identify a parameter range capable of producing PBHs. We then expand our analysis to a more comprehensive IPT scenario, incorporating non-zero top-quark mass effects within the STU model, and discover that PBH formation can be significantly influenced by the STU parameters. Furthermore, we find that PBHs can be effectively constrained by their impact on the universe's matter density, particularly through the cosmic microwave background radiation, while the STU parameters can be restricted by the non-standard effects on the Higgs boson potential. We develop a framework that incorporates an additional reward function into reinforcement learning to promote solutions with a certain intrinsic characteristic - a low fractional dimension - by minimizing the action's magnitude. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to various domains, including continuous-time systems, optimal control, and continuous-time Markov decision processes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework by adapting it to continuous-time systems and using it to solve a trajectory tracking problem for an unmanned ground vehicle while minimizing motion. This results in a substantial reduction in action intensity - up to 42% - and movement duration, achieving a fractional dimension of 0.56. We also demonstrate that our framework can handle constraints on motion smoothness and terminal positions, maintaining a fractional dimension of 0.54. Furthermore, we show that our framework can be integrated with existing methods to promote diverse solutions and reduce the risk of convergence to local optima. Our framework is available as an open-source Python library. We believe that our research has the potential to inspire novel applications, including the development of motion planners that minimize motion artifacts, and provide a foundation for future research in fractional dimension-based trajectory optimization. privacy challenges.

The concept of probabilistic fairness has emerged as a more inclusive approach to counterbalance the effects of biased decision-making processes. Unlike traditional notions of fairness, which focus on individual outcomes, probabilistic fairness aims to promote the overall well-rounded experience. The underlying idea is to strike a balance between group and individual outcomes, ensuring that the system remains fair on average. In this paper, we develop a new framework for testing probabilistic fairness across various scenarios, including binary, continuous, and high-dimensional settings. The proposed test is grounded in empirical research, drawing inspiration from the classic Bernoulli inequality. The results demonstrate that the test is reliable, even when the underlying distribution is unknown, and can be applied effectively. Furthermore, empirical studies confirm that the test is robust and can be successfully used in real-world applications. The proposed test is also adaptable to situations where the goal is to detect the presence of probabilistic unfairness rather than ensuring fairness. A Cox process is an advanced point process model that's widely used to analyze count data in non-standard distributions. It's an adaptable model that's particularly useful for capturing the patterns of irregular events. In this study, a Cox process was used to model the occurrence of earthquakes in relation to tectonic plates, specifically focusing on the impact of plate boundaries on earthquake frequencies. To analyze this relationship, a bivariate approach was employed, considering the earthquake data in both spatial and tectonic contexts. We utilized a Gaussian interaction function to model the impact of plate boundaries on earthquake patterns, and our results showed that while earthquakes primarily occur near plate boundaries, they also occur in the gulf of Persia due to the presence of a rigid crust. Furthermore, our model suggests that plate boundaries contribute to approximately 60% of earthquake activity in the study area. Furthermore, our findings also show that non-Markovian dynamics can mitigate the negative consequences of strong interactions between the system and the environment, thereby preserving quantum coherence in the system. The theoretical results are supported by numerical simulations. In addition, our research also explores the optimal conditions under which the anti-Zeno effect becomes most pronounced. The study's outcomes have significant implications for the development of quantum technologies based on superconducting qubits. We also discuss the relationship between the total mutual-visibility number and the total visibility number of Cartesian product graphs. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for the total mutual-visibility number of Cartesian products of trees and prove that a graph has a total mutual-visibility number of one if and only if it is a tree. Additionally, we investigate the graphs with $\mu^*_{\text{tv}}(G) = 2$ and derive a formula for $\mu^*_{\text{tv}}(G)$ for some specific graphs. The results presented in this paper are new and provide insights into the properties of Cartesian product graphs. The proofs are original and contribute to the understanding of the total mutual-visibility number of Cartesian product graphs. A crucial step in the pruning process involves determining which model parameters to eliminate. Most current pruning methods make local decisions about individual parameters based solely on their contribution to a specific training task. In contrast, we propose a multi-faceted approach that considers a parameter's broader role in the network, including its interactions with multiple devices and resources such as storage and processing power. This is achieved by treating parameter reallocation as a mixed integer linear program that optimizes network efficiency across multiple tasks. Our approach has been successfully tested on a range of tasks such as image classification, object detection, and natural language processing, and has outperformed existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational complexity. Notably, we have demonstrated that our method can reduce model size by up to 37% while maintaining similar accuracy as the original model. Our findings also show that our method can be effectively applied to real-time systems with strict latency constraints. Overall, our research suggests that parameter pruning should be viewed as a problem of optimizing resource allocation across multiple tasks rather than a single task-specific objective. This is particularly relevant in the context of embedded systems where network efficiency is critical. Our code has been made publicly available for further research and development. Complex-valued neural networks, particularly used in speech and image processing, have shown benefits over their real-valued counterparts. Federated learning, specifically personalized federated learning, addresses the challenge of machine learning in data federations by developing models tailored to each user's needs. This approach overcomes the limitations of centralized learning, which requires central data aggregation, by locally training separate models on each device, resulting in numerous locally trained models with poor inter-user generalization. Our experiments show that this approach can effectively improve model generalization across various scenarios. Moreover, we demonstrate that this approach can also be enhanced by incorporating transfer learning, resulting in even better performance. This research contributes to the field of personalized federated learning by offering a new method to improve model generalization and presenting an innovative approach using hypernetworks. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive study of how to improve personalization through transfer learning, and we make our code available for public use. This study investigates the impact of accountability on the performance of data scientists. We designed a system that automatically tracks and evaluates their predictions, providing personalized feedback. By comparing the results of automated assessment with those of human evaluators, we found that the automated system is equally effective and efficient. As for motivation, we observed that the tool had a positive effect on participants' desire to share their findings with others, as well as their interest in learning more about data ethics. Nevertheless, we noted that the tool had no significant effect on ethics-related discussions or self-reported confidence levels. The tool's potential to facilitate accountability was also tested in a leadership setting, where team leaders who received training on data ethics led teams utilizing the accountability tool. We discovered that this leadership intervention led to an increase in the use of proper ethical labels in project reports, although this effect was only significant when coupled with a monetary incentive. Overall, our research aimed to provide a framework for understanding how motivation and accountability are interconnected in the context of data ethics. Ultimately, we hope to contribute to a greater understanding of data ethics by exploring the underlying psychological mechanisms of accountability and motivation. We introduce a complete definition of the crystalline cohomology for any scheme with two dimensions or less, leveraging the foundational work of Scholze on axiomatic formalism, as well as the research by Binda, Bieri, and Bieri-Schochet-Berthelot on etale and crystalline cohomology. This development enables us to demonstrate the existence of a p-adic Riemann-Hilbert correspondence for smooth schemes of two dimensions or less. We also establish a connection between p-adic Riemann-Hilbert for smooth schemes of one dimension or more and the log crystalline cohomology of their unit tangent bundle. This development offers a p-adic substitute for Bhatt-Scholze's log p-adic Hodge-Tate conjecture, which has been previously formulated in the context of perfect stacks. This study investigates the work distribution and associated entropy production for a particle submitted to external driving under the influence of stochastic return. We derive the exact distribution of work done on the particle by exploiting the path-integral representation of work fluctuations. Notably, we find that the work distribution exhibits a double exponential form, with the exponent influenced by a parameter representing the stochastic return frequency. We then analyze the corresponding entropy production and identify specific conditions under which the large deviation theory remains valid. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the third-order cumulant of work remains unchanged by stochastic return frequency. Our analysis is supported by numerical simulations. Additionally, we extend our findings to a Brownian particle in a potential well under stochastic return, and provide an expression for the work distribution in this context. We validate these results through Monte Carlo simulations. This study contributes to the understanding of work fluctuations in systems with stochastic return, and highlights the role of stochastic return in modifying work statistics. Moreover, it reveals the robustness of the third-order cumulant of work fluctuations in the presence of stochastic return. Our results have implications for the study of nonequilibrium systems and may be relevant to the design of molecular machines. Specifically, they suggest that molecular machines with stochastic return may exhibit distinct work statistics compared to those without. Ultimately, this study aims to shed light on the role of stochastic return in modifying work statistics in molecular machines. We introduce gvnn, a novel neural network library that specializes in geometric vision, offering advanced tools like multi-view loss functions, sophisticated cost functions, and built-in self-calibration capabilities for network optimization. By integrating self-calibration, our framework ensures networks remain robust against scale and translation variations without needing additional pre-processing or modification. Through a self-calibration feature, users can easily fine-tune networks for specific tasks, such as metric reconstruction, or simplify more complex tasks, like 3D object detection, by breaking them down into more manageable components. By streamlining the process and making it easier to implement, our framework makes geometric vision tasks more accessible to users. gvnn is built on top of PyTorch, making it easy to integrate with existing machine learning tools, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by showcasing its performance on various vision tasks, including 3D detection, and achieving superior results compared to previous methods. The development of Reinforcement Learning algorithms heavily relies on the accuracy of reward functions, which are notoriously difficult to craft for complex real-world tasks. This paper investigates the effects of flawed reward specifications on RL agents and proposes a method to detect such issues. It also aims to determine if agents can be modified to achieve performance comparable to those designed with accurate reward functions. Through experiments, we assess the impact of reward misspecification on RL agents and evaluate the feasibility of correcting their behavior. Our results indicate that agents designed with incorrect rewards can still produce satisfactory outcomes with behavior modification, as determined by two proposed metrics. A significant number of IoT applications require complex computations that cannot be handled by individual devices, thus necessitating offloading to cloud servers or edge devices. However, cloud-based offloading faces limitations in terms of bandwidth and latency, while edge devices may lack sufficient storage capacity. To address these challenges, this paper proposes Self-Serviced IoT, an architecture that empowers users to offload computations to local machines, ensuring seamless and efficient operation. This study introduces an innovative controller for a tethered aerial robot that guides humans through physical interaction. The controller considers the human's position and movement in decision-making processes, taking into account both the human's speed and proximity to the robot. Moreover, the human's comfort level is improved when the robot moves at a constant pace, indicating a potential trade-off between interaction effectiveness and comfort. These findings highlight the need for a balanced approach to robot movement control in physical human-robot interaction scenarios. Our research also provides valuable insights for designing safe control systems for robots interacting with humans in real-world settings. This study investigates the representation of Uralic language characteristics within a shared linguistic space using a multilingual word embedding framework. We examine how well these models capture various language features such as the presence of case markers, vowel harmony and agglutinative characteristics across different languages. Our analysis reveals that these models can accurately identify and associate with specific language traits when provided with sufficient linguistic data. Furthermore, our findings indicate that these word embeddings are more effective than traditional methods at distinguishing the Uralic languages from Indo-European languages, suggesting they are more suitable for language classification tasks. Our research also explores the potential of these models to identify novel language relationships and to generate new language connections within a network. However, our attempts to use these models to separate Uralic and Indo-European languages were unsuccessful, as they failed to outperform traditional methods based on basic linguistic features. Additionally, our efforts to use these models to separate Uralic languages into distinct subfamilies were also unsuccessful, as the models were not able to identify any clear language subgroups. We attribute these limitations to the limited availability of data on Uralic languages and the models' sensitivity to data quality. Overall, our research highlights the value of using word embeddings to analyze linguistic patterns and the potential of these models to provide new insights into language relationships. However, our findings also emphasize the need for further research to fully realize the potential of these models in linguistic analysis. Epidemic models are being increasingly used to forecast the spread of infectious diseases and evaluate the effectiveness of containment measures. However, these models are often limited by the need for extensive data, which can be difficult to obtain, especially during the initial stages of an outbreak. This research presents a novel approach that leverages a genetic algorithm to identify optimal model parameters for an SIR-type epidemic model in the absence of detailed data. By utilizing available information such as the cumulative number of cases and dates of implementation for non-pharmaceutical interventions, the model can be optimized to accurately forecast future outbreaks. By applying this method to early-stage COVID-19 data from Algeria, the researchers were able to develop a predictive model that forecasted the subsequent 14 days of cases with a high degree of accuracy. The study's findings suggest that the implementation of non-pharmaceutical interventions significantly reduced the number of new cases, and that the model accurately captured the dynamics of the early epidemic, providing valuable insights into the spread of the disease in Algeria. The proposed approach has the potential to be applied to other countries in the absence of detailed data, and could serve as a valuable tool for public health officials in the early stages of an outbreak. This study introduces a novel technique for robotic object manipulation within unstructured environments, utilizing a particle-based approach that learns object properties and action strategies through self-supervised learning. By employing a physics engine to simulate object behavior, our method generates visual feedback to train a policy network that maps object configurations to effective grasps. This approach enables robust manipulation of complex objects with irregular surfaces, even when viewed from a single perspective, as it does not rely on pre-existing action heuristics or object segmentation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in creating generalizable policies for manipulating objects with a wide range of shapes and sizes. Furthermore, our particle-based policy can be adapted to real-world applications, such as the manipulation of 3D printed objects, as shown by its successful application on a robotic arm. We have conducted a comprehensive investigation into the magnetic properties of Nd$_2$(Zr$_{1-x}$Ti$_x$)$_2$O$_7$ pyrochlore magnets through a combination of experimental and theoretical methods. Our research revealed that these materials exhibit a complex magnetic phase diagram influenced by both crystal-field symmetry and spin-orbit coupling. Specifically, we found that a critical distortion of the crystal-field splitting occurs at a threshold of approximately 0.2 for the 10% Ti-doped samples, resulting in a complex magnetic phase diagram with multiple critical points. This paper explores the feasibility of model checking for programming languages with advanced memory management capabilities.  By utilizing a sequence of events and relying on a partial order of data updates, we establish a fundamental framework for checking the correctness of programs that operate under relaxed memory rules.  The framework effectively accounts for the indirect effects of memory updates on dependent operations, and it ensures that programs are evaluated accurately across different memory configurations, including a standard, synchronized memory model and more complex, asynchronous memory models.  Furthermore, we illustrate the practical application of this approach by using it to verify key properties of programs that operate under relaxed memory rules, and we demonstrate its ability to work effectively with conventional programming constructs, such as locks and atomic blocks, by translating them into sequences of events.  The framework also supports the creation of abstract programs that are semantically equivalent to their original counterparts, and it effectively handles the introduction of synchronization mechanisms, including locks and atomic blocks, into these abstract programs.  The paper also includes a detailed case study of this approach in action, involving the development of a concurrent library for memory management that is based on a sequence of events. Finally, it emphasizes the need for designers to thoroughly test their mechanisms in real-world scenarios, even those involving less common market fluctuations, to ensure their mechanisms operate effectively in unexpected circumstances. Hyperspectral images are highly valuable for remote sensing applications due to their numerous benefits, but they are often marred by noisy data that hinders their full potential. To overcome this limitation, a novel denoising technique is presented in this research, leveraging the intrinsic connections between adjacent spectral bands to produce superior results. The proposed method employs a spatial-spectral cross attention network that effectively incorporates long-range interactions between neighboring spectral bands. The network's cross attention module, comprising a spatial attention block and a spectral attention block, is designed to selectively weigh the importance of noisy data and neighboring spectral bands. The spatial attention block is tailored to handle spatial correlations, while the spectral attention block is designed to handle correlations between neighboring spectral bands. Through extensive experiments on various datasets, the proposed method has outperformed existing state-of-the-art denoising techniques in terms of performance metrics. The authors investigate the energy-critical semilinear heat equation involving a heat equation with critical Sobolev growth and bounded initial conditions: 
  \begin{equation*}
  \partial_t
  u-\Delta u =|u|^{2^*}, \quad t\in(0,\infty),\quad x\in\mathbb{R}^N,
  \end{equation*}
  where N is greater than one and the initial conditions satisfy $0\leq u_0\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and $u(0)=u_0$.
  Previous research by Wei and Seregin and Piovesio showed that global solutions cannot be extended beyond a finite time when the initial conditions are small enough.
  In this work, the authors refine their analysis of blowup solutions by using a local approach, which allows them to rule out Type II blowups and establish a new criterion for the formation of singularities in finite time, given by the condition
  \begin{equation*}
  \sup_{0<t<\infty}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_t|^2\,dx\right)^{\frac{N-2}{(N-2)^2)}}
  <\infty.
  \end{equation*}
  This result implies that small data solutions cannot blow up in Type II.
  In the process, the authors develop a new local Liouville theorem, which provides a key tool to understand the nature of blowup solutions. 
  Additionally, the authors investigate the long-term behavior of solutions that blow up in finite time and show that they converge weakly to a nontrivial ground state solution of the stationary problem when the initial conditions are small enough. 
  This result holds under a slightly weaker condition than the criterion for the formation of singularities. 
  Furthermore, the authors establish that solutions that blow up in finite time with large data do not converge weakly to a nontrivial ground state solution of the stationary problem. 
  This result holds under the assumption that the formation of a singularity occurs at a finite time, which is a stronger condition than the criterion for the formation of a singularity. 
  Finally, the authors provide an example of an initial condition that satisfies the criterion for the formation of a finite-time singularity but does not satisfy the criterion for the formation of a large-data blowup.

This paper's primary objective is to establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity and present various implications. To achieve this, the authors leverage the concept of uniform ellipticity for sets of elliptic operators, which was initially introduced by Dallakian (2009). Building on this foundation, the authors expand upon Dallakian's work by demonstrating that a given elliptic operator is uniformly elliptic on a specific set if and only if that set can be represented as the level set of a harmonic function. This result has far-reaching consequences, including a significant finding: for a given second-order elliptic operator P in R^n and a real number lambda greater than 1, the set of points where P satisfies the inequality |Px| <= lambda times det(Px) is equivalent to the level set of a harmonic function. This conclusion has significant implications, including a novel proof of Dallakian's theorem on uniformly elliptic sets, an alternative approach to deriving the Hamilton-Jacobi equation for a specific type of dynamical system, and a characterization of weakly convex functions in terms of the level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that a function is weakly convex if and only if it satisfies a specific inequality involving the divergence of a tensor field, and they extend and generalize a key result in the theory of mean curvature flows. The authors also explore the applications of their findings to the study of the large-time behavior of mean curvature flows, the study of the first eigenvalue of a specific type of operator, and the theory of optimal transport. Finally, they propose several open problems for further investigation. Computer model predictions are often hampered by uncertain input parameters and approximations, casting a veil of uncertainty over their accuracy. Calibration techniques aim to rectify this by adjusting parameters to align with experimental data. However, when a computer model falls short of physical plausibility, traditional calibration methods prove inadequate. This study proposes a novel approach that incorporates physically informed prior distributions into Bayesian calibration to enhance model performance. The method is demonstrated using a diffusion equation with experimental data, showcasing its potential to yield more accurate predictions and a refined uncertainty analysis compared to a simple uniform prior. The research also explores the interplay between model performance, calibration, and uncertainty, as well as the potential limitations of the proposed technique. The findings suggest that this method can be a valuable addition to the calibration toolbox, particularly when dealing with computationally expensive models. A new public data set called NapierOne has been developed to support research in data analytics and natural language processing. This mixed file dataset offers an updated alternative to Govdocs1 and is available for download under an open license. NapierOne is comprised of over 1.9 million documents from 2019, representing over 1.8 billion pages and 15.9 terabytes of text data. Its diverse content includes 1,100 different file types and over 300 metadata fields, with text encoded in various formats across multiple fields. This data set is unique in that it contains a range of file formats, with over 80% of its files represented as images, PDFs, or Microsoft Word documents. NapierOne is designed to provide a more challenging test bed for developing text analysis systems than its predecessor, with a higher proportion of non-text files requiring the removal of images and other non-text content. To validate the effectiveness of NapierOne, a basic text extraction system was developed and trained on a large portion of the data, with its performance evaluated on the remaining documents. This research presents the development of NapierOne, the challenges posed by its diverse file types, and the results obtained from training and testing a basic text extraction system on this new dataset. This research introduces an innovative approach to calculating the cosmological power spectrum, which significantly reduces the computational time required for the non-linear Hubble evolution and the non-linear growth of structures. By transforming the problem into an optimization task with a unique objective function, the method utilizes the adjoint technique to optimize the integration of the Boltzmann equation and the Schrodinger equation. This optimization allows the calculation of the power spectrum using a single forward simulation, thus significantly reducing the computational cost. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by applying it to the 1-step FLRW model and the 2-step non-linear Hubble and structure evolution model, and we observe that the computational time is reduced by a factor of 10 to 100. This method has the potential to be applied to more complex models in the future. Additionally, we discuss the challenges associated with the non-linear Hubble and structure evolution model and the potential strategies for addressing these challenges. This method has the potential to be used in conjunction with other cosmological simulation methods in the future. Moreover, the proposed method's implementation is straightforward, requiring only a brief period of training via back-propagation and a minimal number of adjustable parameters. The paper includes an example comparison with a well-established polynomial filter, illustrating the benefits of the proposed method. The example involves a second-order filter, yet it is capable of achieving smoothing quality comparable to that of the polynomial filter, albeit with a more complex structure. The proposed method's potential applications include robotic motion control, autonomous vehicle navigation, and other trajectory planning tasks. The presented approach is also versatile and can be applied to various fields, including robotics, computer vision, and autonomous systems. This research introduces FMM, a novel R package facilitating the analysis and interpretation of rhythmic patterns within biological oscillators. By utilizing a wavelet-based approach, FMM extracts rhythmic signatures from experimental data, specifically identifying patterns of periodicity, phase, and amplitude. Experimental data can comprise either time series data or phase-shifted measurements. FMM's capabilities include the analysis of rhythmic patterns, model fitting, parameter estimation, and model evaluation. Notably, the package can also synthesize simulated data, enabling users to evaluate the performance of model fits. FMM's methodology is demonstrated through its application to cardiac pacemaker cells, as well as to astrocytic gap junctions and synaptic connections in neuronal networks. FMM is available for public access via GitHub (https://github.com/JuliaR package/FMM). Further information and documentation can be found at https://fmm-package.github.io/FMM.
